name: topiary
desc: Uniform formatter for simple languages, as part of the Tree-sitter ecosystem
why: Driven by Tree-sitter queries that describe formatting as data, a neat look at how code formatters are built.

brief.what_it_is: Topiary is a uniform code formatter for simple languages, built on the Tree-sitter parsing ecosystem and written in Rust by Tweag. Formatter authors describe a language's style in a simple DSL, and Topiary's engine applies that style to source code, so authors do not need to write their own formatting engine or parser. End users get one formatter tool that can apply a consistent style across several languages. The README does not spell out the exact input and output formats, and the homepage only points to the Book for usage.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames the problem as subjective personal style choices that waste hours of review time. It positions Topiary as a "universal formatter engine" that lets developers auto-format codebases uniformly and lets language authors define a style quickly, provided a Tree-sitter grammar exists for that language.
brief.how_it_works: The README says the style is defined in a simple DSL and that Topiary relies on Tree-sitter for parsing, so a formatter author does not write a grammar. The README does not describe the mechanism in detail. The scout note says formatting is driven by Tree-sitter queries that describe formatting as data, but the fetched pages do not confirm that wording, so treat it as unverified.
brief.install_notes: The fetched README and homepage show no install commands, and the Book's installation page returned 404 at the URL I guessed. The homepage says to see the Topiary Book for installation and usage, so the brief writer should check the Book or the latest release page for install steps. Nothing in the fetched text mentions hardware, accounts, runtimes, or configuration.
brief.standout: Formatters are usually built from scratch with a dedicated parser and engine per language. Topiary instead lets an author describe a language's formatting style in a small DSL on top of an existing Tree-sitter grammar, so a new formatter needs only the style rules. Its stated design goals also include idempotency, preserving the author's line-spanning choices, and keeping diffs local to the lines that changed.
brief.status: Probably maintained, but I could not confirm it. The README has live-looking release and CI status badges and a Discord link, and the homepage links to a "Latest release" and blog posts. I did not see a release date or last-commit date in anything I fetched, so the status is best described as unknown with weak signs of activity.
brief.caveats: The README says the tool is aimed at "simple languages", so it is not a general answer for complex ones. Its ability to match existing community styles is an aspiration in the design principles, not a guarantee. The fetched pages do not list supported languages, platforms, or licence. The Book's installation page was not reachable at the URL I tried. The brew description and scout note mention queries, which the fetched text does not confirm.
quotes: Topiary aims to be a uniform formatter for simple languages, as part of the Tree-sitter ecosystem.
Authors can create a formatter for a language without having to write their own formatting engine or even their own parser.
Expect idempotency. That is, formatting of already-formatted code doesn't change anything.
Topiary aspires to be a "universal formatter engine"
